old: Whether this Madhavacharya and the famed monk **Vidyaranya** were one and the same person, or two distinct individuals, remains genuinely debated. Some scholars firmly hold they are identical; others find this doubtful without offering a strong counter-case. Most of the works discussed here are attributed to Madhavacharya, and it is well-established that Madhavacharya, minister to Vijayanagara's founding kings, holds the central historical role — a question examined in detail by Sriman Hastavakal Krishnamachari's article in *Indian Historical Quarterly* (Vol. VI, pp. 701–717), which weighs the evidence on whether "Madhavacharya" and "Vidyaranya" name one figure or two across his ministerial and later monastic careers.
new: Whether this Madhavacharya and Vidyaranya are one and the same person, or two different persons, is a very important question; the problem is still unsolved. Some scholars are very doubtful that these are two names of one person. Though some of their arguments look strong, even works contemporary with Madhavacharya, not only later ones, bear witness that Vidyaranya and Madhavacharya, the minister of the early kings of Vijayanagara, are identical. But in the Indian Historical Quarterly (Vol. VI, pp. 701–717) it is determined, on the evidence of inscriptions, that this Madhavacharya or Vidyaranya and the Madhava who was minister of Bukka I (known in history as Madhava-mantri or Amatya Madhava) are different persons. They too appear to have been eminent scholars like Vidyaranya.
basis: Kannada p.248: sandehavullavaru (doubtful, not firm); abhinnarembudakke sakshibhutavagive; Indian Historical Quarterly ... bere bere vyaktigalendu shasanagala adharadinda nirdharisalpattide; English added Krishnamachari
